requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists as a shared writable directory with correct ownership/permissions (mode 1777, root:root)
requirements.summary: mkdir + chmod 1777 applied; stat/ls confirmed drwxrwxrwt root:root both before and after restart.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users (sticky-bit enforcement) while remaining able to create their own files
requirements.summary: dropuser1 created file1.txt; dropuser2's rm attempt failed with 'Operation not permitted' while dropuser2 could still write its own file2.txt. Re-verified with a fresh file post-restart.

requirements.requirement: Configuration is durable/persistent (survives a restart) and directory is on persistent storage
requirements.summary: findmnt confirmed /srv is on XFS-backed /dev/vda3 (not tmpfs). A full node restart was performed: pre-restart boot_id 96974ac3... captured with directory healthy, systemctl reboot issued, connection dropped and reconnected, post-restart boot_id 2089ebb0... confirmed different, and both the 1777/root:root permissions and sticky-bit delete-denied behavior were re-verified live afterward. This satisfies the bounded disruption+recovery evidence bar.

requirements.requirement: Test artifacts (throwaway users, test files) cleaned up, leaving /srv/drop empty and correctly configured
requirements.summary: Test files removed after each check; dropuser1/dropuser2 accounts (and their processes) were removed after a first userdel attempt failed due to lingering processes, then pkill+userdel succeeded. Final ls -la shows /srv/drop empty with correct mode/ownership.

overall_summary: The executor correctly configured /srv/drop as a 1777 root:root shared directory and functionally verified sticky-bit semantics (deletion blocked for non-owners, creation allowed for all) both before and after a full node restart, with boot-identity evidence confirming the restart actually occurred and configuration/behavior persisted. Test users and files were cleaned up, leaving the directory in its final correct empty state. The only blemish is a small leftover /tmp/reboot.log file from the reboot mechanism that was never removed.
limitations: The reboot connection-drop window (cmd-4234eb90c5af4e66, cmd-4b846ae948794a34, cmd-2159781febb44210) only shows timeouts/connection-reset, not direct evidence of the node being fully down; this is standard/expected behavior for a remote reboot and not treated as a gap.
/tmp/reboot.log leftover was not directly inspected for content, only confirmed present in the after-executor temporary-files snapshot.

operational_hygiene.summary: Actions taken (mkdir/chmod on /srv/drop, creating two test users, writing/removing test files, systemctl reboot) all had a clear, evidence-supported role in configuring or verifying the sticky-bit directory, and the test users/files were fully removed by the end (cmd-5a7b19db07c04b8e, cmd-7aa2ed7b9bb14976). No unnecessary or unrelated mutations were found. One minor residue: the nohup reboot redirect created /tmp/reboot.log (cmd-71ffd417663b4170), which is still present in the after-executor temp-files snapshot and was never cleaned up — a low-risk, low-impact leftover file but technically an unremoved artifact of the restart mechanism. No failed/conflicting services, no weakened security controls, no damaged package state observed in before/after snapshots.
